authoredSolutions.67: \(BQ=d;\ \tan60^\circ=30/d\Rightarrow d=10\sqrt3.\) \(\tan15^\circ=(30-PQ)/d\Rightarrow PQ=30-10\sqrt3(2-\sqrt3)=60-20\sqrt3.\) \(BCPQ\) is a rectangle of area \(d\cdot PQ=10\sqrt3(60-20\sqrt3)=600(\sqrt3-1).\)
authoredSolutions.70: Cayley-Hamilton: \(A^2=aA-bI\) with \(a=\text{tr}A,b=|A|.\) \(A^2=I\Rightarrow aA=(1+b)I.\) If \(a\ne0\), \(A\) is scalar (diagonal), contradicting all \(a_{ij}\ne0\); so \(a=0\Rightarrow b=-1.\) \(3a^2+4b^2=0+4=4.\)

authoredSolutions.152: S1: \(2023^{2022}-1999^{2022}\) is divisible by \(2023-1999=24\), hence by 8. True. S2: \(13\cdot13^{n}-11n-13=13^{n+1}-11n-13\). Since \(13^{k}\equiv1+12k\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 144)\), \(13^{n+1}\equiv12n+13\), so the expression \(\equiv (12n+13)-11n-13=n\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 144)\), divisible by 144 whenever \(n\) is a multiple of 144 — infinitely many. True.
authoredSolutions.153: Each factor \(\big(2^{1/2}-2^{1/(2k+1)}\big)\in(0,\sqrt2-1)\), and \(\sqrt2-1\approx0.414<1\). An infinite product of positive factors each bounded above by a constant \(<1\) tends to \(0\).
authoredSolutions.154: Let \(z=x+iy\), \(u=x^2-y^2\). \(\mathrm{Re}(az^2+bz)=au+bx=a\), \(\mathrm{Re}(bz^2+az)=bu+ax=b\). Multiply by \(a,b\) and subtract: \((a^2-b^2)u=a^2-b^2\Rightarrow u=1\) (as \(a\neq b\)). Subtracting the two equations gives \((a-b)(u-x)=a-b\Rightarrow u-x=1\Rightarrow x=0\). Then \(x^2-y^2=1\Rightarrow -y^2=1\), impossible for real \(y\). No solution: \(0\) elements.
authoredSolutions.155: With \(\lceil x\rceil\) the smallest integer \(\ge x\), \(\lceil x\rceil-x\in[0,1)\), positive except at integers. Domain \(A=\mathbb{R}-\mathbb{Z}\). Range: \(\lceil x\rceil-x\in(0,1)\Rightarrow 1/\sqrt{\,\cdot\,}\in(1,\infty)\), so \(B=(1,\infty)\). S1: \(A\cap B=(1,\infty)\) minus integers \(=(1,\infty)-\mathbb{N}\), true. S2: \(A\cup B\) includes non-integers below 1, so it is not \((1,\infty)\); false. Only S1 true.
authoredSolutions.156: Put \(v=x\log_e x\), so \(\dfrac{dv}{dy}=(1+\log_e x)\dfrac{dx}{dy}\). The equation becomes \(\dfrac{dv}{dy}-v=e^{y}\), giving \(v e^{-y}=y+C\Rightarrow x\log_e x=(y+C)e^{y}\). Through \((1,0)\): \(0=C\Rightarrow x\log_e x=ye^{y}\). At \((\alpha,2)\): \(\alpha\log_e\alpha=2e^{2}\), i.e. \(\log_e(\alpha^{\alpha})=2e^{2}\Rightarrow \alpha^{\alpha}=e^{2e^{2}}\).

authoredSolutions.179: Hyperbola \(2x^2-2y^2=1\) has \(e_h=\sqrt2\), so ellipse \(e=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\Rightarrow a^2=2b^2\). Orthogonal intersection of a central ellipse and hyperbola means they are confocal. Ellipse foci\(^2=a^2-b^2=b^2\); hyperbola foci\(^2=\tfrac12+\tfrac12=1\Rightarrow b^2=1,a^2=2\). Latus rectum \(=\tfrac{2b^2}{a}=\sqrt2\), squared \(=2\).
